title: The Spirit Poured Out, the Idol Mocked, Cyrus Named
summary: God promises to pour out his Spirit on Jacob's descendants, so that people will gladly claim the LORD's name. He declares that he is the first and the last and there is no other Rock, and then the prophet paints a long satire of a man who burns half a log to cook his dinner and bows down to the other half. The chapter ends with God's call to Israel to return, a burst of praise from all creation, and a sweeping declaration that names Cyrus as God's shepherd who will see Jerusalem and its temple rebuilt.
story: Chapter 43 ended with Israel's sin and God's willingness to blot it out. Chapter 44 begins with “But now,” and the promises grow larger: not just release from Babylon but the outpouring of God's Spirit and a new generation eager to belong to him. The long satire of idol-making in the middle of the chapter is the sharpest in the Bible, and it prepares for the climax. For several chapters a conqueror from the east has been mentioned without a name. Now, in the final verse, God names him: Cyrus. The reader moves from what God is like, to what idols are like, to what God is about to do in history.
historical:
Cyrus II, the Great, ruled Persia from about 559 BC until his death in 530 BC. After conquering the Medes and Lydia, he took Babylon in 539 BC, reportedly with little resistance. In 539/538 BC he permitted exiled peoples to return to their homelands and rebuild their temples. A clay cylinder found at Babylon in 1879 (the Cyrus Cylinder, now in the British Museum) records his policy of restoring displaced peoples and their gods, though it does not mention the Judeans. The biblical record of his decree for the Jews appears in Ezra 1:1-4 and 2 Chronicles 36:22-23. Returning exiles laid the foundation of the second temple in the years after the decree (Ezra 3), and it was completed around 516 BC.

The naming of Cyrus here, in 44:28 and 45:1, is the most discussed detail in the authorship debate over Isaiah. If Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote it around 700 BC, Cyrus is named about a century and a half before his rise. The first-century Jewish historian Josephus preserved a tradition that Cyrus himself read these words and was moved by them to issue his decree. The competing positions are set out in the hard question below.
cultural:
The satire of verses 9 to 20 describes real crafts with precise detail. A blacksmith works over coals with hammers, a woodworker marks out his figure with a line, a stylus, and a compass, and the finished statue is given human form and placed in a shrine. The tree itself is planted and watered by rain that God sends. In Babylon, cult statues were made by skilled artisans and then ceremonially brought to life, and worshipers believed the god now dwelled in them. The prophet deliberately ignores that ritual and looks only at the wood: the same log that bakes bread and roasts meat becomes the god a man prays to.

Writing “The LORD's” on the hand (verse 5) likely draws on the practice of marking slaves or soldiers with their master's name, and perhaps on the custom of marking property. Here the mark is gladly taken. Jeshurun (verse 2) is a rare poetic name for Israel, found elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32 and 33, probably meaning upright one. Calling Cyrus a shepherd applied an old royal title to a foreign king.
literary: The chapter opens with an oracle of salvation (verses 1 to 5) and a trial speech (verses 6 to 8), both familiar from chapters 41 to 43. The satire of verses 9 to 20 is the chapter's heart. It moves slowly and with heavy irony, repeating “half of it” and “the rest of it,” and reaches its point in the idol-maker's prayer, “Save me, for you are my god.” A brief call to return (verses 21 and 22) and a hymn of praise (verse 23) follow. The final section (verses 24 to 28) is a single long sentence in Hebrew, a string of participles describing the LORD as the one who makes, stretches, foils, confirms, says. It builds from the creation of the heavens to the rebuilding of Jerusalem and ends on the name of Cyrus, the chapter's surprise.

outline.t: The Spirit poured out on Jacob's descendants
The first and the last: there is no other Rock
Return to Me, for I have redeemed you
The LORD who made all things names Cyrus

doctrines.note: “I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants.” The Spirit brings life like water on dry ground, and its fruit is people who freely claim the LORD as their own. The promise joins the prophets' expectation of a future outpouring of the Spirit (compare Joel 2:28-29; Ezekiel 36:26-27).

The satire exposes idolatry as self-deception. The worshiper cannot see that the thing in his hand is a lie, because he has made a god of what he himself controls. The chapter traces the blindness to the heart: “His deluded heart has led him astray.”
God directs the course of empires to accomplish his purposes. Cyrus, a pagan king, will “fulfill all that I desire” without knowing the one who called him.

words.note: Pesel, carved image or idol, from a verb meaning to cut or hew. The word appears four times in this chapter. The same term is used in the second commandment's prohibition of carved images (Exodus 20:4). The satire shows why: the carved thing can only be as great as the carver.

Tsur, rock. “There is no other Rock; I know not one.” In Deuteronomy 32 and the Psalms, the title names God as a place of refuge and stability. The idols of verses 9 to 20, wood that burns and statues that must be nailed down, are the opposite of a rock.

Sheqer, lie or deception. The satire ends with the question the idol-maker cannot bring himself to ask: “Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?” The word describes what is false and misleading, not just mistaken.

Koresh, Cyrus, the Persian king. His name appears in the Old Testament in Isaiah, Ezra, Chronicles, and Daniel. In Isaiah it comes only twice (44:28; 45:1), at the climax of a long argument that the LORD alone announces events before they happen.

christ: The promise to pour out the Spirit on Jacob's descendants belongs to a family of prophetic promises that the New Testament sees fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured out on Jesus's followers (Acts 2, which quotes Joel). The connection to Isaiah 44 is thematic rather than a direct citation. The title “the first and the last,” which God claims here as proof that there is no God besides him, is spoken by the risen Christ in Revelation 1:17 and 22:13. And Cyrus, called God's shepherd and in the next chapter his anointed, is a pagan king used to free God's people. The New Testament does not treat Cyrus as a type of Christ, but readers have noticed the pattern: God raises up a deliverer to release captives and rebuild his house. Christ is presented as the true shepherd (John 10) and the one who builds God's true temple (John 2:19-21).

hard.q: How could a prophet in the eighth century BC name Cyrus, who lived about 150 years later?
hard.a:
This is the sharpest form of the authorship question. Readers who hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book say that he did so by revelation, and that the naming of Cyrus is not an embarrassment to the text but its argument: throughout chapters 41 to 48, God proves his deity by announcing events before they happen, and the naming of Cyrus is the climax of that claim. They note a parallel in 1 Kings 13:2, where Josiah is named long before his birth, and point to Josephus's tradition that Cyrus read these words himself.

Most critical scholars conclude that chapters 40 to 55 were written by a prophet during the exile, when Cyrus was already conquering the region, and that the prophet interpreted his rise as God's doing before the fall of Babylon in 539 BC. On this view the prophecy is still a genuine word from God, but it speaks into events already under way. Some mediating readers hold that the book grew within Isaiah's tradition and was shaped into its present unity over time. Readers of all these views agree on the chapter's claim: the God of Israel, not the gods of Babylon, stands behind the rise and fall of empires.

questions: The idol-maker could not ask, “Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?” What things do people trust today that they would find it hard to question?
God says “I will never forget you” and then calls, “Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.” Why do you think redemption comes before the call to return?
God used a pagan king to rebuild his temple. How does that challenge assumptions about whom God can use?
